passage: At the colony summer camp in Chennai, the leader shook a cloth bag of caps. "Close your eyes and pick!" Mridul, five, pulled out orange. His neighbour Sumit got purple. The oranges jumped in a huddle. "Orange is the smartest!" Mridul shouted, though nobody had found any treasure yet. When the leader said, "Hold hands with a partner," Mridul would not take Sumit's hand. "You're purple." Sumit, who shared his cycle with Mridul every evening, looked at his cap and then at Mridul. At the end the leader collected the caps. Mridul held his tight behind his back.

qa.q: How did the children get their caps?
qa.a: The leader shook a cloth bag and each child closed their eyes and picked one.

qa.q: How can you tell Mridul already feels he belongs to the orange group?
qa.a: He feels proud of being orange, shouting that orange is the smartest before any treasure is found and holding his cap tight when the caps are collected.

qa.q: What could the camp leader do when Mridul refuses Sumit's hand?
qa.a: The leader could remind them the caps came out of a bag by chance and pair oranges with purples for the next game, so the children mix again.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit when Mridul won't hold his hand?
qa.a: Sumit is confused and probably hurt, because the two share a cycle every evening and now a cap he picked by chance has turned him into an outsider.

grounding: A five-year-old given a cap colour by chance quickly decides his colour is best and treats a friend in the other colour as 'them'.

passage: "Papa, I'm a Star!" Usha waved her hand. A shiny sticker sat on it. "A star? What for?" "For the Stars team. We're the best team." "Best at what?" "Everything." Usha climbed onto her chair. "The Moons are silly." Papa passed the dal. "Is Imran a Moon?" "Yes." "But you sit with Imran every day." Usha frowned. "Not today. Stars sit with Stars." "How did you become a Star?" "Miss gave stickers from a box. I got a star." "So if you got a moon?" Usha looked at her sticker. "Then... Moons are the best?" She did not sound sure.

qa.q: What was on Usha's hand when she came to the table?
qa.a: A shiny star sticker was on her hand.

qa.q: Why does Usha frown when Papa says she sits with Imran every day?
qa.a: She feels torn, because she likes Imran but now believes Stars should only sit with Stars.

qa.q: Which question from Papa helped Usha stop and think, and why?
qa.a: Asking what would happen if she had got a moon made her see the teams came from a box by chance, so being a Star is not what makes someone best.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Usha would not sit with him?
qa.a: Imran might have felt left out and puzzled, since they sit together every day and nothing changed except a sticker.

grounding: A young child given a team sticker at random quickly believes her team is best and stops sitting with a friend from the other team.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: At the community centre's kabaddi tournament, Trisha, ten, wore the green club shirt like a second skin. When her club lost the final by a single raid point, she sat on the bench with her fists pressed into her eyes. It felt as if the other club had beaten her, not the team. Then the winners began to dance. Their captain, Deepika, had a loud laugh and a gap in her teeth. "Gap-tooth Deepika!" Trisha called, and made a face. Her teammates hooted and copied her. Deepika's little sister, sitting on the steps, stopped clapping and started to cry. The coach walked over. Trisha's stomach turned. She was still proud of green. She just wished she hadn't said it.

qa.q: By how much did Trisha's club lose the final?
qa.a: They lost by a single raid point.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she sat on the bench after the loss?
qa.a: She felt personally hurt, as if the other club had beaten her, which is why she pressed her fists into her eyes.

qa.q: What could Trisha do now that her stomach has turned?
qa.a: She could go to Deepika and her little sister, say sorry for the nickname, and congratulate the winners while still being proud of her own club.

qa.q: How does Deepika's little sister experience the moment Trisha makes fun of Deepika?
qa.a: The little sister's happy clapping turns to tears, because a proud moment for her sister has become a joke about her teeth.

grounding: A girl is personally hurt by her club's loss, and her group pride slips into mocking the rival captain.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: I'm Lavanya, and I sit next to Charu in Class 5. Charu is in Blue House and talks about it all year. On sports day she tied blue ribbons in both plaits and made a paper flag. When Yellow House won the relay by a whisker, Charu sat down on the grass and did not get up for the prize-giving. I don't know if she was crying; she kept her face in her knees. The next morning, before the teacher came, Charu drew a fat yellow duck on the board and wrote "YELLOW CAPTAIN" under it. Some boys laughed. Mitali, the Yellow captain, walked in and saw it. Charu looked at Mitali's face, then quickly rubbed the board with her sleeve. She didn't say much at lunch.

qa.q: What did Charu draw on the board?
qa.a: She drew a fat yellow duck and wrote 'YELLOW CAPTAIN' under it.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling when she quickly rubbed the board clean?
qa.a: She probably felt sorry or embarrassed once she saw Mitali's face, realising the joke had hurt a real person.

qa.q: How could a teacher support Charu after this?
qa.a: A teacher could praise her love for Blue House, talk quietly with her about how Mitali felt, and help her make a proper apology.

qa.q: How might Mitali see Charu when she walks in and finds the drawing?
qa.a: Mitali might feel singled out and embarrassed, and see Charu as someone who could not bear Blue losing.

grounding: A girl whose house loses feels deeply hurt, and her pride turns into mocking the rival captain, as seen by a classmate.

passage: "Why's Sahil banging doors?" Mummy asked. Dolma didi didn't look up from her book. "Riverside lost again. Relegated." Sahil stomped in. "It's not funny." "I didn't laugh." "You were going to." He threw himself on the sofa. "Everyone at school will say our city can't even keep a football team." "So?" "So it's us. It's me." Dolma put her book down. "Honestly, their defence has been rubbish all season." "Don't say that!" Sahil sat bolt upright. "You don't even watch them!" "Sahil, I'm talking about eleven players, not you." "It's the same." Mummy sat beside him. "Last month when they won the derby, you were singing in the shower for two days." Sahil said nothing. His ears were red. "You're allowed to love them," Dolma said more gently. "You're just not them."

qa.q: What happened to Riverside, according to Dolma?
qa.a: Riverside lost again and was relegated.

qa.q: Why does Sahil sit bolt upright when Dolma criticises the defence?
qa.a: He feels hurt and defensive, taking the criticism as an attack on himself because he believes the team's loss makes the city, and him, look bad.

qa.q: Which line from Dolma could help Sahil most, and why?
qa.a: 'You're allowed to love them. You're just not them' lets him keep his love for the team while separating his own worth from its results.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Sahil's reaction?
qa.a: She sees him taking a football result as a personal insult, and at first finds it a bit silly, then speaks to him more gently.

grounding: A teenager's mood soars and crashes with his city's football club, and he reacts to criticism of the team as if it were aimed at him.

passage: I'm Ishita. At fifteen, my school's name was stitched into who I was. When the city newspaper ranked us second for board results, I walked about like the proudest girl in the corridor. The next year we slipped to sixth, and my mood slipped with it. I couldn't eat lunch properly. Then someone on an online forum called our school "a rote factory", and I spent till two at night replying to strangers. My friend Pranav, from another school, joked, "Relax, your school isn't your mother." I didn't talk to him for a week. Looking back, what hurt wasn't the ranking. It was that I'd let the school's name hold my own sense of being good enough. I still love my school. I just keep a bit of myself outside it now.

qa.q: Where did someone call Ishita's school 'a rote factory'?
qa.a: Someone called it that on an online forum.

qa.q: Why did Pranav's joke upset Ishita so much at fifteen?
qa.a: Because her sense of being good enough was tied to the school, so a joke about it felt like an insult to her.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ishita keep her pride without being ruled by it?
qa.a: Looking back and seeing that the ranking only hurt because she let the school's name hold her self-worth, she chose to keep part of herself outside it.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt during the week Ishita didn't talk to him?
qa.a: Pranav might have felt confused and shut out, since he meant a light joke and suddenly lost a friend's company over it.

grounding: A teenager's mood rises and falls with her school's ranking, and she defends it fiercely because insults to the school feel like insults to her.

qa.q: How did Leela feel after the senior's comment about her accent?
qa.a: She felt reduced to just that one thing for two days, which suggests she was hurt and a little resentful.

qa.q: What choice does Leela make now that she sees her different identities?
qa.a: She chooses to remember the nurse, the chess player and the sadya expert, so one snide comment cannot define her.

qa.q: How might Seema see Leela's realisation?
qa.a: Seema seems to see it as a healthy change and is glad Leela has a way to shrug off one person's remark.

grounding: A student notices that different identities come forward in different company, and seeing this keeps one label from taking over.

passage: In the village near Akola, everyone called Vaibhav "the college boy" the moment he got off the bus with his agriculture textbooks. Uncles asked him about seed prices as if he were an expert. At the college hostel, it was the opposite: there he was "the farmer's son," the one who knew how cotton actually smelled. And on Sunday evenings at the kabaddi ground, he was simply the best raider on the left side. His cousin Indu laughed when he told her. "So which one are you?" Vaibhav, twenty, thought about it while they walked back past the well. "All of them. Whichever the people around me notice first." Last month a hostel senior had sneered at "village boys," and it had stung for days. Now it stung less. He was a village boy. He was also three other things.

qa.q: What did the uncles in the village ask Vaibhav about?
qa.a: They asked him about seed prices as if he were an expert.

qa.q: Why does the hostel senior's sneer sting Vaibhav less now?
qa.a: Because he has realised he is several things at once, so being called a village boy no longer feels like the whole of him.

qa.q: Which choice in how Vaibhav sees himself helps him, and why?
qa.a: It lets him own being a village boy with pride while knowing no single label, good or bad, gets to take over.

qa.q: How might Indu see her cousin differently after the walk?
qa.a: Indu might see that Vaibhav changes a little depending on where he is, and that this is not being fake but having many true sides.

grounding: A student sees himself as a college boy, a farmer's son or a raider depending on who is around, and noticing this keeps any one label from dominating.

passage: I'm Ujjwal. Last year our small software firm was bought by a bigger one, and suddenly there were "old" people and "new" people on the same floor. I'm from the old side. For the first month I ate lunch only with my old team. When a new colleague missed a deadline, I heard myself say, "Typical new lot." Nobody said it was wrong, which made it worse. Then Kishore, from the new side, stayed back till ten helping me fix a server crash that wasn't even his. "Go home, bhai, I'll watch the logs," he said at one point, and I didn't. Walking to the auto stand, we realised we lived in the same part of town and supported the same cricket team. The next morning I split our project tasks by skill, not by which company people came from. I'm still proud of what our old team built. I just stopped needing the new people to be worse.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal hear himself say when a new colleague missed a deadline?
qa.a: He heard himself say, 'Typical new lot.'

qa.q: What did Ujjwal realise about his own attitude, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ujjwal realised the old team was being favoured, shown by eating lunch only with them, and felt uneasy that nobody challenged the 'Typical new lot' remark.

qa.q: Which choice by Ujjwal treated people more fairly, and why did it help?
qa.a: Splitting project tasks by skill rather than by company judged everyone on their work, which loosened the old-versus-new line.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Ujjwal after that night fixing the server?
qa.a: Kishore might see him as a colleague and neighbour rather than someone from the other side, and feel more at home on the floor.

grounding: After a merger a young adult catches himself favouring his old team, finds shared ground with a new colleague and treats both sides fairly, keeping pride without contempt.

passage:
League coordinator's note, 14 October. Written by Ms Kaur.

Chinmay, twenty-four, volunteers as an assistant referee and still plays for Northside FC. Today he was assigned Northside against Eastbank, their fiercest rivals. I watched him closely. When a Northside player went down near the box, the Northside bench screamed for a penalty. Chinmay kept his flag down: it was a clean tackle. His old teammates booed him. Afterwards, Eshaan, the Eastbank captain, came over to thank him. Chinmay said, "You'd get the same from me any day. We're all the same league." Then he suggested something I had never heard from either side: a joint training morning for the under-twelves of both clubs.

My next step: I've booked the ground for that morning and asked Chinmay and Eshaan to run it together.

qa.q: Which teams played in the match Chinmay helped referee?
qa.a: Northside FC played Eastbank, their fiercest rivals.

qa.q: What did Chinmay seem to be thinking when he kept his flag down despite the booing?
qa.a: He seemed focused on being fair to both sides and willing to accept his teammates' anger rather than favour his own club.

qa.q: Why was suggesting a joint training morning a good next step?
qa.a: It builds a wider shared identity, one league and one set of young players, so the rivalry does not turn into contempt.

qa.q: How might Northside players feel about Chinmay after the match?
qa.a: Some may feel betrayed at first, but over time they might trust that he calls games honestly, including when it helps them.

grounding: A young volunteer referee resists favouring his own club, treats the rival fairly and builds a wider shared identity across clubs.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: "Ujjwal bhaiya, Neha's house has a lift inside the building. And she got a new bicycle with gears." Parveen, ten, dropped her school bag. "And a phone. Her own phone." "Okay," said Ujjwal, peeling an orange. "We don't have anything." "We don't have anything?" He pointed at the orange. "What's this?" "You know what I mean." "No, tell me." Parveen flopped onto the mat. "Her room is pink and big." "Your room has the bookshelf Abbu built." "Hers has a TV." "You watched two films this week." "On the family TV." Parveen's voice wobbled. "I just felt small there." Ujjwal handed her half the orange. "Were you hungry this morning? Cold last night?" "No." "So what's missing?" Parveen chewed slowly. "Nothing. It just looked like less, next to hers."

qa.q: What did Neha get, according to Parveen?
qa.a: Neha got a new bicycle with gears and her own phone.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when she came home from Neha's house?
qa.a: She felt small and a little sad, because next to Neha's things her own life suddenly seemed like less.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the talk with Ujjwal?
qa.a: When Ujjwal asked what was actually missing, Parveen saw that nothing was; her hurt came only from comparing.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see his sister's complaint?
qa.a: He sees that she has everything she needs and patiently helps her notice it, without mocking her feelings.

grounding: A ten-year-old who has enough feels poor after seeing a friend's new bicycle and phone, and realises the hurt came from comparison.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: I'm Sarita. When I was nine, my friend Himani got a new red bicycle and a phone for her birthday. I remember riding home on my old cycle, which worked perfectly, and feeling like the poorest girl in the world. I didn't want to ride with Himani any more. I told her I was busy. At home I had my own shelf of storybooks, a cricket bat and a mother who made rajma every Sunday. None of that seemed to count. Then my little cousin Nitin visited and stared at my bookshelf. "You have so many books," he whispered. "You're so lucky." I looked at my shelf the way Nitin did. Nothing in my house had changed. I had only been looking at Himani's things instead of mine.

qa.q: What did Himani get for her birthday?
qa.a: She got a new red bicycle and a phone.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel riding home on her old cycle?
qa.a: She felt envious and small, like the poorest girl in the world, even though her cycle worked perfectly.

qa.q: What changed Sarita's mind, and what could she do next?
qa.a: Seeing her bookshelf through Nitin's eyes showed her how much she had, so she could start riding with Himani again.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when Sarita kept saying she was busy?
qa.a: Himani might have felt puzzled and a bit lonely, not knowing that her new bicycle was the reason her friend stayed away.

grounding: A child who has enough feels poor next to a friend's new bicycle and phone, and later sees the sadness came from comparison, not lack.

passage: "Deepika, can I say something awful? I'm fifth in class. Fifth, out of forty-two. And I've been miserable for a week." Trisha pulled her knees up on the bench. "Because my whole group is one to four. Ananya's first, you're third. I'm the girl who's 'also in the group.' And it's not just marks. For the farewell party, everyone's getting new outfits stitched. Mine is Didi's old lehenga, which is actually lovely. But next to theirs it felt like a hand-me-down, which, okay, it is. Last night I cried and told Mummy it wasn't fair. She said, 'What isn't fair? You're fifth.' I couldn't explain. If I'd been in a group of kids ranked twentieth, I'd be the star. Same marks. Same lehenga. It's just who I'm standing next to. Isn't that stupid?"

qa.q: What rank is Trisha in her class?
qa.a: She is fifth out of forty-two.

qa.q: Why has Trisha been miserable for a week?
qa.a: She feels cheated and left behind because the friends she compares herself with are ranked one to four and have new farewell outfits.

qa.q: What could Trisha do with the insight she already reached?
qa.a: She could remind herself who she is measuring against, and look at how far she has come or at Didi's lovely lehenga for what it is, rather than next to her friends'.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel hearing Trisha say this?
qa.a: Deepika might be surprised, since fifth sounds excellent from where Deepika sits, and might feel a little awkward to be one of the people Trisha compares herself to.

grounding: A teenager with good marks and a decent outfit feels cheated because she compares herself only with friends a step ahead.

passage: I'm Tushar, Omkar's older brother, and I watched this happen at his under-sixteen cricket camp. Our parents had saved for months to buy him a proper willow bat for his birthday. He slept with it next to his pillow for two nights. Then he took it to camp. Three of the boys there, all a bit better than him, had full branded kits: helmets, pads, bags with their names stitched on. That evening Omkar put the bat in the corner and didn't oil it. When Papa asked about camp, he said, "It's fine," in a flat voice. At dinner he muttered, "Everyone else gets proper stuff." Papa looked at the bat in the corner and didn't say anything. I can't be sure what Omkar was thinking. But the bat hadn't changed. Only the boys next to him had.

qa.q: Where did Omkar sleep with his new bat for two nights?
qa.a: He slept with it next to his pillow.

qa.q: What does Omkar's flat 'It's fine' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt let down and cheated after comparing his bat with the better kits of the boys a step ahead of him.

qa.q: What could Tushar do to help Omkar see his bat differently?
qa.a: Tushar could oil the bat with him and remind him how he felt on his birthday, before he started measuring it against the others' kits.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he hears Omkar say everyone else gets proper stuff?
qa.a: Papa might feel hurt and quietly sad, since the family saved for months for a bat that now sits unoiled in the corner.

grounding: A teenager who got a good bat feels deprived after comparing himself with slightly better-equipped teammates, as seen by his brother.

passage:
Thursday

The nursing recruitment exam has been postponed AGAIN. Third time. No new date.

Every single senior from the batch above me got a government hospital post straight after the results. Zainab's batch, every one of them. They'd tell us in the canteen, "Don't worry, it's automatic." I topped my practicals. I did everything they did, and more. And now I'm working night shifts at a small clinic for half the pay while the seniors post photos in their new uniforms.

I'm so angry I can't sleep. It feels like someone took my post and put it in a drawer.

Zainab called tonight. She said, "Rehana, it's not personal. It's the timing." I snapped at her. Then I felt terrible. It isn't her fault she got hers.

But it isn't mine either that I didn't get mine.

qa.q: How many times has the recruitment exam been postponed?
qa.a: It has been postponed three times.

qa.q: What does Rehana mean by writing that someone took the post and put it in a drawer?
qa.a: Rehana feels bitter and as if something earned and was owed is being withheld.

qa.q: What could Rehana try after snapping at Zainab?
qa.a: Rehana could call Zainab back to apologise, and then look at what can be prepared while waiting, instead of letting anger at the seniors fill the nights.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt when Rehana snapped at her?
qa.a: Zainab might have felt hurt, since she was trying to comfort Rehana, and a little awkward about having got a post herself.

grounding: A young graduate who expected a post like the batch above feels bitter and entitled when it does not come, especially seeing the seniors' success.

passage: Devika, sit. You're new at managing, so let me tell you about my first year on the floor at the garment unit. I was twenty-four. That summer the company put new standing fans and padded stools in the cutting section. Stitching got nothing. Pay was the same for both, fair pay, above the other units in the area. But within two weeks the stitching women stopped talking to the cutting men at tea. Someone scratched "cutting = kings" on the stitching room door. I noticed and, at first, I thought, they're being childish. Then I asked why the fans went to cutting. Nobody had told us: the cutting room had been measured as the hottest. So I got the measurements, showed them to both sections, and got a date in writing for stitching's fans. Listen to an old man, beta. Your team can swallow a lot. What they can't swallow is not knowing why. - Wasim

qa.q: What did the company put in the cutting section that summer?
qa.a: It put new standing fans and padded stools in the cutting section.

qa.q: What did Wasim first think when he noticed the resentment, and how did that change?
qa.a: At first he thought the stitching workers were being childish, but after asking why the fans went to cutting he realised nobody had explained the reason.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Wasim handled it?
qa.a: Getting the heat measurements, showing them to both sections and securing a written date for stitching's fans made the rule visible and fair.

qa.q: How did the stitching workers experience the new fans in cutting?
qa.a: They felt left behind and treated as less important, even with fair pay, which showed in the silence at tea and the words scratched on the door.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment in one section when another gets perks despite fair pay, and eases it with clear criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: The quarterly review was on Monday, and Himani, twenty-six and managing the day shift at the call centre, had one weekend to deal with the mood on her floor. Since the company started a free cab for the night shift, her day team had gone cold. Pallavi, usually the first to help new joiners, now sat with her headphones on at lunch. On Friday Himani heard her mutter, "Night shift gets cars, we get nothing." Everyone was on the same pay scale. Then the rain started and half her team was stuck at home, so there was no chance of a meeting. Himani asked HR for the cab rule in writing: it was for safety after midnight. She put it in one clear message to the team, with the pay scale beside it, and added the shift allowance day staff could apply for. On Monday Pallavi took her headphones off at lunch.

qa.q: What did the company start for the night shift?
qa.a: It started a free cab for the night shift.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's muttered comment suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels left out and resentful, as if the day shift is valued less, even though pay is the same.

qa.q: What did Himani do well despite the rain keeping her team at home?
qa.a: She got the cab rule in writing and sent one clear message explaining the safety reason, the equal pay scale and an allowance day staff could apply for.

qa.q: How might the night shift have seen the day team's coldness?
qa.a: The night shift might have been confused or hurt by it, since the cab was for their safety after midnight, not a reward.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment when one shift gets a perk despite fair pay, and reduces it with transparent criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: The staff room went quiet when the principal pinned up the notice: Hrithik Sir, head of the science department. Tejas, twenty-five, who had joined the school the same year, kept marking Class 8 notebooks. His red pen pressed so hard it tore a page. Hrithik came in, and Tejas said, "Congratulations," in a voice he barely recognised. At break he stood by the water cooler and made himself ask, silently: what do I actually have? A job he loved, children who stayed back to ask questions, the science club he started. What can I control? Finishing his B.Ed. project, and asking the principal what the post needed. Three years ago he had been tutoring in a rented room. He still wanted to lead a department one day. He went back and asked Hrithik if the science club could use the lab on Fridays.

qa.q: What post did Hrithik get?
qa.a: He became head of the science department.

qa.q: What does Tejas's red pen tearing a page suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is fuming with envy and frustration, even while keeping quiet in the staff room.

qa.q: Which choice by Tejas helped him most, and why?
qa.a: Asking himself what he has, what he can control and where he was three years ago let him keep his ambition without letting envy take over his day.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Tejas when he asks about the lab on Fridays?
qa.a: Hrithik might be relieved that Tejas is working with him rather than against him, and more willing to support the science club.

passage:
Dear Baljeet Paaji,

You asked in your last letter how the new job is going. Honestly, last Monday I almost wrote to you in a rage. Arun, who joined the kitchen a month after me, was made sous chef. I spent the whole dinner service slamming pans.

Then I remembered what you told me when I was washing dishes at your dhaba: "Count what's in your hands before you count what's in someone else's." So I did. I have a job in a proper hotel kitchen. The head chef trusts me with the tandoor. I've learned three new sauces this year. What can I control? My knife speed, which is still slow, and asking chef what Arun did that I didn't. And four years ago I couldn't make a round roti.

I still want that sous chef coat. I'm just not angry about it any more.

With respect,
Lokesh

qa.q: Who was made sous chef?
qa.a: Arun, who joined the kitchen a month after Lokesh, was made sous chef.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel on the Monday Arun was promoted?
qa.a: Lokesh was furious and envious, so angry that the whole dinner service went in slamming pans.

qa.q: What helped Lokesh turn that anger into something useful?
qa.a: Remembering Baljeet's advice, Lokesh counted what was in hand, named what could be controlled and looked back four years, keeping the goal without the anger.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Baljeet would likely feel proud that Lokesh remembered the advice from the dhaba days and used it to handle a hard moment.

grounding: A young cook fuming at a peer's promotion looks at what is in hand, what can be controlled and how far the journey has come, and keeps ambition without envy.
